Example: “We adapt [cited work]’s encoder for multi-domain inputs.” (7) EvaluateAgainst : The citing work explicitly compares its own findings and results with those of the cited work, typically to establish effectiveness. Example: “Our model outperforms [cited work]’s method on F 1 F_{1} score.” These citation intent types are designed to be mutually exclusive, which can be combined with content types for multi-dimensional interpretation. By structurally separating citation intent from cited content type, SOFT resolves ambiguities common in one-dimensional frameworks. For example, citing a model without applying it is annotated as Contextualize:ProducedResource , while referring to an unresolved issue is SignalGap:Discovery . Only when the citing author explicitly acts, e.g., reuses, modifies, justifies, or critiques, is an active intent assigned. This orthogonality supports consistent labeling across citation contexts and improves annotation reliability. SOFT’s two-dimensional design also enhances downstream applications. Separating gap signaling from design justification enables clearer modeling of research motivation. Distinguishing between using a tool ( Use:ProducedResource ) and referencing a methodological trend ( Contextualize:PerformedWork ) supports finer-grained tracking of scientific influence, method lineage, and intent-aware scientific recommendation. As demonstrated in Section 5 , the SOFT framework yields higher human–LLM agreement, better classification performance, and improved generalizability across scientific domains.
